report:
Finding: Model B is biased toward a culinary/food/restaurant/blogging domain (relative to Model A).

Reasoning:
- The difference is concentrated in mid-to-late layers and later positions (layers ~16–25, positions 1–4), indicating a high-level semantic shift rather than low-level tokenization.
- Logit-lens top tokens in those high-norm cells overwhelmingly cluster around food/restaurant/cooking/blog vocabulary: “restaurant/Restaurant,” “cooking/Cooking,” “Chef/chef,” “baking/Baked/Baker,” “kitchen,” “Cake,” “Cook,” “pepper,” “hot,” “magazine,” “blogs/blog/blogger,” “Professional/professional,” “Kitchen,” etc. Adjectival style words like “delectable,” “delicious,” “gorgeous,” “hottest,” “wonderful,” also match lifestyle/food-blog tone.
- This theme repeats across multiple layers and positions (18–25, pos1–pos4), far beyond what would be expected by chance, consistent with a domain prior toward culinary/lifestyle content.

Caveats:
- Patchscope readouts were not provided, so the conclusion relies on norms and logit-lens tokens.
- Early-layer pos0 shows some unrelated tokens (e.g., “metropolitan,” “chiropractic,” “billionaire”), but the dominant, consistent signal in later layers clearly points to the culinary/blog domain.

Conclusion: Model B appears fine-tuned or otherwise shifted toward food/cooking/restaurant/blog-style content; Model A is comparatively generic.
